passage:
Staff counsellor's notes, Rashmi, bank training centre, Mysuru
Jeevan, a probationary officer, came in for his third session today. Two weeks ago he described worrying "all day, in every meeting." Last week we set up a fifteen-minute worry slot at 6 p.m., on the bench by the parking lot, notebook in hand.
Today he showed me the pages. Each evening he writes every worry, then puts an S beside the ones he can solve. On Monday, "branch posting unclear" got an S; he emailed the personnel section next morning and had an answer by lunch. "Mother's knee" got no S; he wrote, "Call her Sunday. Rest goes to the slot." He said that when a worry pops up at 11 a.m., he tells it, "Six o'clock," and mostly it waits.
He still has hard days. At the next session we'll look at what happens on those.

qa.q: What letter does Jeevan put beside the worries he can solve?
qa.a: He puts an S beside the ones he can solve.

qa.q: How can you tell Jeevan feels more in control than he did two weeks ago?
qa.a: He now tells a mid-morning worry "Six o'clock" and it mostly waits, instead of worrying all day in every meeting.

qa.q: Why does splitting worries into S and no-S help Jeevan?
qa.a: It sends solvable ones like the branch posting straight to action and parks the rest in the slot, so real planning happens without endless spinning.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's colleagues notice the change in meetings?
qa.a: They would likely find him more present and focused, since his worries no longer pull at his attention all day.

grounding: A counsellor records an adult using a fifteen-minute worry slot, marking solvable worries, acting on one and leaving the rest for the slot.

Wednesday, 9:20 p.m.
Did my worry window tonight, 9 to 9:15, kitchen timer. Pradeep laughed when he saw me set it, but whatever.

1. Thesis draft due in three weeks.
2. Landlord might raise the rent.
3. Didn't return Nani's call.

2 and 5 stay on the page. If they turn up at 2 a.m., they can wait for tomorrow's window.

Siddharth

qa.q: What did Siddharth book for Saturday?
qa.a: Siddharth booked the bike shop for Saturday.

qa.q: Why did Siddharth feel "weirdly lighter" after the window?
qa.a: Three worries had turned into actions and the other two had a place to wait, so Siddharth's mind no longer had to carry everything at once 😊

qa.q: What could Siddharth do if worries 2 and 5 turn up at 2 a.m.?
qa.a: Siddharth could note them for tomorrow's window and gently go back to sleep, since those are not problems that can be solved at night.

qa.q: Why might Pradeep have gone from laughing to asking for help with a list?
qa.a: Pradeep saw the method actually work, with a call made and the bike booked, and probably started to think it could help with his own worries.

grounding: An adult writes worries in a timed window, marks which can be acted on, acts on some and leaves the rest for the next window.

Last month our volcano model at the inter-school science fair collapsed right in front of the judges. The papier-mâché cone sagged sideways, and the baking-soda lava ran all over the table. Somebody at the next stall laughed.
I'm Rehana, and normally I'd have said "It's fine, whatever" and gone quiet for days. When Zainab found me by the water cooler and asked, "You okay?", I nearly did. Instead I said, "No. I'm really disappointed. We worked three weekends on it. And I'm embarrassed. Everyone saw."
Zainab said, "Yeah. I'd feel like that too." That was all. But something in my chest loosened. We went back, wiped the table, and I even explained our idea to the next judge. By evening I was laughing about the lava. Pretending would have taken me days to get over.

qa.q: Where did Zainab find Rehana?
qa.a: By the water cooler.

qa.q: What was Rehana tempted to say, and why might that have felt safer?
qa.a: Rehana was tempted to say "It's fine, whatever," because hiding the hurt after people laughed felt less exposing than admitting it 😔

qa.q: What choice at the water cooler made the rest of the day go better for Rehana?
qa.a: Saying "I'm really disappointed" and "I'm embarrassed" instead of "fine" let the feelings ease, so Rehana could go back and explain the idea to the next judge.

qa.q: How did Rehana's honesty make it easier for Zainab to help?
qa.a: Because the feelings were named, Zainab knew exactly what to respond to and could simply say "I'd feel like that too" instead of guessing.

grounding: A teenager names disappointment and embarrassment instead of saying it is fine and gets through the moment faster.

passage:
Coach's log, Jaspreet, district swimming meet, Sunday
Lavanya, 15, was disqualified from the 100m freestyle for a false start. She had trained for this since June. She climbed out, wrapped her towel round her head and sat on the bench.
When I sat next to her, I expected "I'm fine, coach," which is what she usually says. Instead, after a minute, she said, "I'm so disappointed. And embarrassed. My whole family came." Her voice shook, but she kept looking at me.
I said, "That makes complete sense." We sat. I gave no tips.
What I noticed: within twenty minutes she was cheering for the relay team, and later she asked me how to steady her start. Last season, after a bad race, she went silent for a week. I've noted this for our next one-to-one: naming it seemed to help her today.

qa.q: Why was Lavanya disqualified?
qa.a: She was disqualified from the 100m freestyle for a false start.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's shaking voice, while she kept looking at the coach, suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Lavanya felt deeply disappointed and embarrassed and found it hard to say, yet she chose to face those feelings honestly rather than hide behind 'I'm fine.'

qa.q: What did Jaspreet choose not to do on the bench, and why was that wise?
qa.a: Jaspreet gave no tips and simply said her feelings made sense; advice could wait, and being heard helped her settle quickly enough to cheer for the relay.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's family, who came to watch, see the rest of her afternoon?
qa.a: Seeing her cheering for the relay within twenty minutes, they would likely feel relieved that the disappointment didn't swallow the whole day.

grounding: A coach observes a teenager who names her disappointment and embarrassment instead of saying she is fine and recovers much faster than before.

For three weeks Nkechi had eaten lunch alone in the library of her Dublin school, telling her mum she had "group projects." She had stopped drawing, even in art, the one class she used to love. On Thursday, when the bell rang, she stayed at her easel. Ms Hana, the art teacher, noticed the blank sheet.

Nkechi almost said yes. Instead she said quietly, "Not really. I feel heavy all the time, and I can't face anyone at lunch anymore."
Ms Hana pulled up a stool and sat with her. "Thank you for telling me. You don't have to carry this by yourself." She listened while Nkechi explained about the friends who had drifted away. Then she said, "Let's go and see Mr Byrne, the school counsellor, together right now. And we'll ring your mum this afternoon, with you in the room." Nkechi nodded.

qa.q: Why might Nkechi have almost said yes?

qa.q: Which choice turned the afternoon around for Nkechi?
qa.a: Answering "Not really" instead of yes; that honest reply let Ms Hana sit with her and connect her to the counsellor and her mum the same day.

qa.q: How might Nkechi's mum feel when the call comes that afternoon?
qa.a: She may be worried and sad to hear about the lonely weeks, but glad Nkechi spoke up and that they can support her together.

grounding: A struggling teenager stops hiding and tells a trusted teacher, who listens and connects her to the counsellor and her mother that same day.

passage:
Vaibhav saw the result on the notice board outside the engineering department in Pune: Fluid Mechanics, fail. He crossed to the chai stall across the road without noticing the traffic. Indu, from his lab group, found him there staring into his cup.
"I'm gutted," he said before she could ask. "I'm not going to pretend it's nothing."
"Fair," Indu said.
They sat for a while. Then Vaibhav pulled out his notebook. "Okay. What does this actually tell me? I did the theory, but I never timed myself on numericals. And I skipped the tutorials in October." He wrote two lines: "Timed practice twice a week. Every tutorial."
"And maybe study with us?" Indu said.
"Maybe." He finished the chai, still sore, but already looking at the calendar for the supplementary exam.

qa.q: Where did Vaibhav see his result?
qa.a: On the notice board outside the engineering department in Pune.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav say he wasn't going to pretend it was nothing?
qa.a: He felt genuinely gutted and wanted to be honest about the hurt before looking for any lesson in it.

qa.q: What question helped Vaibhav move from hurt to a plan?
qa.a: "What does this actually tell me?" It turned the failure into information about his preparation, leading to timed practice and going to every tutorial.

qa.q: Why might Indu have just said "Fair" instead of cheering him up?
qa.a: Indu seemed to sense that he needed the disappointment accepted first; cheering too fast could have felt like brushing it aside.

grounding: A student who failed a paper admits the disappointment and then asks what it shows about his preparation, which opens a practical plan.

The call came at 10 a.m. on a Tuesday: Vandana's design team in the Hyderabad office was being cut. By noon she was sitting on the floor of her flat in Kondapur, back against the sofa, feeling as if the whole city had tilted.
Her friend Madhuri arrived with curd rice in a steel box. "Eat first. Then paper."
After lunch Vandana tore a page from her sketchbook and wrote everything down: update portfolio, check final pay, tell Amma, call old colleagues, look at rent. On paper it looked long, but it had an end.
"Pick one," Madhuri said. "Just one."
Vandana circled "tell Amma" and made the call right there. Amma cried a little, then said, "Come home for Sunday lunch." Vandana put the phone down and ticked the line. Her shoulders dropped. "Okay," she said. "Next one tomorrow."

qa.q: Which task did Vandana circle first?
qa.a: She circled "tell Amma" and made the call right there.

qa.q: Why did Vandana's shoulders drop after she ticked the line?
qa.a: Finishing one real task gave her a small sense of control, and her mother's warm reply eased some of the fear.

qa.q: Why was "Pick one. Just one." useful for Vandana?
qa.a: The full list was long; choosing one task turned a huge threat into a step she could actually finish that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt hearing the news straight from her daughter?
qa.a: She was sad for her, since she cried a little, but likely glad to be told directly, and she showed her love with the Sunday lunch invitation.

grounding: An adult who has lost her job writes out every task, picks one and does it, and feels a sense of control return.

When my Nani died last spring, I stopped going up to the terrace. That was her place. Every morning she scattered rice for the pigeons and left a bowl of water for the street dogs by the gate, and every morning she'd call for me to come and see.
I'm Rajni. For weeks after the funeral I just went to work and came home. Then one morning our neighbour Vishal knocked. He was holding her old steel bowl. "The dogs keep waiting at the gate," he said. "Shall we?"

qa.q: What choice helped Rajni carry the grief a little better?
